'''Dale Leonard Compton''' (born June 1935) is an American [[aerospace engineer]]. He was the sixth director of [[NASA]]'s [[Ames Research Center]], serving from 1989 to 1994.

==Early life and education==
Compton earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] in aeronautical engineering from [[Stanford University]] in 1957, where he was a member of [[Sigma Nu]].<ref name=":0" /> He also earned a [[Master of Science]] in 1958 as one of the first students taught by former Ames aerodynamicist [[Walter G. Vincenti]].<ref name=":1" /> 

He earned a [[Doctorate of Philosophy|doctorate]] from Stanford in 1969.<ref>{{cite web |title=Measurements of the effective heats of ablation of teflon and polyethylene at convective heating rates from 25 to 420 BTU/FT2 sec. |url=https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/8598025 |website=searchworks.stanford.edu |publisher=Stanford University |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> He was a [[Sloan Fellows|Sloan Fellow]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] from 1974 to 1975 and attended the Advanced Management Program at [[Harvard Business School]] in 1986.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Dale L. Compton - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/people/dale-l-compton/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref>

==Career==
Compton joined Ames Research Center as a [[research scientist]] studying [[aerodynamics]].<ref>{{cite web |title=27th Aerospace Symposium |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19940025124/downloads/19940025124.pdf |publisher=NASA |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> His early work studied [[ablation]] and [[Thermodynamics|aerothermodynamic]] effects on [[Ballistic missile|ballistic missiles]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Administration |first1=United States National Aeronautics and Space |title=NASA Technical Note |date=1959 |publisher=National Aeronautics and Space Administration. |location=Moffett Field, California |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/NASA_Technical_Note/O1PCgjSNFtkC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=dale+l.+compton&pg=RA1-PP1&printsec=frontcover |access-date=20 March 2026 |language=en}}</ref> He was a scientist for fifteen years, contributing to [[Project Mercury]], [[Project Gemini]], and the [[Apollo program]]. 

In the mid-1970s, Compton entered management, serving as deputy director for astronautics. He was later appointed chief of the space science division and manager of the [[IRAS]] telescope project office.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ames Flow Chart |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/orgcharts/83HQorg92-1.pdf |publisher=NASA |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> He was also made director of engineering and [[Computer system|computer systems]] at Ames and named deputy director to [[William F. Ballhaus Jr.]] in 1985.<ref name=":0" /> 

On February 1, 1988, Compton became acting center director of Ames until February 1, 1989, succeeding Ballhaus.<ref>{{cite web |title=Historic Personnel - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/historic-personnel/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> He resumed the position on July 15, 1989, and was formally appointed director on December 20, 1989, the fiftieth anniversary of the center's founding by [[Smith J. DeFrance]].<ref name=":2">{{cite book |title=NASA Activities |date=April 1990 |publisher=The Administration |page=19 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/NASA_Activities/ciV0l2y7pwAC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=dale+l.+compton&pg=RA9-PA19&printsec=frontcover |access-date=20 March 2026 |language=en}}</ref>  

He was considered conservative in his vision for Ames by some at NASA, and even a "tunnel hugger" for believing that Ames' standing at NASA was dependent on its [[wind tunnel]] flight research.<ref name=":1" /> In his view, project-oriented centers went through [[boom and bust]] cycles as [[United States Congress|Congress]] approved or rejected major projects, and Ames could be protected by its specialization. Ames received $300 million in the late 1980s for wind tunnel and simulator restoration projects, which Compton ensured received the highest priority.<ref name=":1" /> Compton also fought for projects conceived at Ames, including the [[Space Infrared Telescope Facility]], [[Mars Observer]], and [[Magellan (spacecraft)|Magellan]], to be executed at Ames, but ultimately lost to the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]].<ref name=":1">{{cite book |title=Atmosphere of Freedom: 75 Years at the NASA Ames Research Center |date=2014 |publisher=NASA History Office |location=Washington, D.C. |pages=18-25 |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/sp-4314-2014.pdf |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> 

In the early 1990s, with the fall of the [[Soviet Union]] and reduction in budget for space research, Compton led the center against efforts to have Ames shut down. He said "Ames has never had a secure place [at NASA]. All directors have tried to secure a place; some have succeeded, some not. My years as director were not easy."<ref name=":1" /> He served as director until his retirement on January 28, 1994, and was succeeded by [[Ken Munechika]].<ref name=":2" /> 

He was recognized by the city of [[Mountain View, California]] in 1994 for his service.<ref>{{cite web |title=City of Mountain View Resolution No. 15652 Series 1994 |url=https://laserfiche.mountainview.gov/WebLink/DocView.aspx?id=19973&dbid=0&repo=CityDocuments&cr=1 |website=laserfiche.mountainview.gov |publisher=City of Mountain View |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> He is a fellow of the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]].<ref name=":0" />

==Awards==
